metadata.file_name: Choose the school  choose the performance  new evidence on determinants of students  performance in eight European countries.pdf
metadata.title: Choose the school, choose the performance: new evidence on determinants of students’ performance in

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD PISA 2018 microdata for eight EU countries (Austria, Croatia, Germany, Hungary, Italy, Portugal, Slovakia, Slovenia) and applies the individual sample weights provided by PISA, as stated in the Data section. The original PISA design is a stratified two-stage sample (schools selected first, then students within schools), so the weighted estimation is intended to restore population representativeness within each country. In the model estimation step, the authors report that standard errors are clustered at the school level, which is consistent with the nested sampling structure (students within schools). The manuscript does not name a specific PISA weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT), and it does not report replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so replicate-weight variance estimation cannot be confirmed from the text.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses PISA 2018 student-level data for the specified eight EU countries. The dependent variables are students’ reading and mathematics scores computed as the average of the ten plausible values. The analytic sample is restricted to students enrolled in school systems where tracking begins at age 15 or before (per the authors’ Eurydice-based country rule). The authors drop observations with missing values on the variables used in the analysis, yielding the final sample of 45,285 students across 2,068 schools.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (OECD, age 15; reading score averaged across 10 plausible values)
main_findings.performance_metrics: OLS with school-clustered standard errors; R-squared reported by country (Total: 0.331; DE: 0.373; HR: 0.358; IT: 0.289; HU: 0.430; AT: 0.315; PT: 0.321; SI: 0.386; SK: 0.389). No ML predictive metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC) reported.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading the study leveraged Number of books at home, School type × city size, and Class size (plus Parental occupational status and Language spoken at home) to explain Reading score, finding that books at home and the school type/localization composite are the most important predictors across countries, while other school characteristics are rarely relevant. This indicates that policies strengthening students’ home learning resources and addressing disadvantages linked to vocational tracking may be more impactful than broad, non-targeted school-level interventions, though the results are correlational and based on OLS with plausible-value score averages.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Mathematics (OECD, age 15; mathematics score averaged across 10 plausible values)
main_findings.performance_metrics: OLS with school-clustered standard errors; R-squared reported by country (Total: 0.325; DE: 0.365; HR: 0.384; IT: 0.283; HU: 0.477; AT: 0.347; PT: 0.341; SI: 0.425; SK: 0.381). No ML predictive metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC) reported.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Mathematics the study leveraged Number of books at home, Parental occupational status, and Class size (and, in some countries, Gender and the School type × city size composite) to explain Maths score, finding that vocational schools perform significantly worse than general schools and that the urban–rural (big vs small city) differences are generally not significant except in Portugal. This indicates that education policy should prioritize reducing inequality associated with vocational tracking and socio-economic background, while urban–rural resource rebalancing may need to be targeted to specific contexts rather than assumed to be uniformly effective.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes OECD PISA 2018 student data for eight EU countries (Austria, Croatia, Germany, Hungary, Italy, Portugal, Slovakia, Slovenia) and models reading and mathematics outcomes using OLS regressions with school-clustered standard errors. The dependent variables are the average of the ten plausible values for each cognitive domain, and the analytic sample (N=45,285) is obtained after dropping observations with missing values on the variables used. For model specification, the authors apply efficient best-subsets selection (Furnival & Wilson) and then estimate effects; they report R-squared by country (e.g., Total R²=0.331 for reading and 0.325 for maths) rather than ML prediction metrics like accuracy or AUC. Across both domains, the strongest predictors are books at home and the school type/localization composite, while vocational tracking is associated with significantly lower performance. The Gelbach decomposition further suggests that family socio-economic characteristics explain most of the general-vocational gap, whereas school quality (notably class size) explains more of the big vs small city gap. Limitations include the absence of explicit survey-weight variable naming and the fact that the approach is predictive/correlational rather than causal.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The paper uses an algorithmic best-subsets selection procedure (Furnival & Wilson) and OLS with clustered standard errors, but it does not train standard machine-learning predictive models (e.g., Random Forest, XGBoost, SVM) and does not report ML prediction metrics. Therefore, ml_techniques.all_techniques is left empty and ml_techniques.primary is null; the study’s “efficient algorithms” are treated as model-selection/estimation procedures rather than ML learners under the schema’s ML algorithm constraints.
